speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION CABINET ASSUME RESPONSIBILITY FOR FAILURE TO CONCLUDE CONTRACT WITH LOCKHEED- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity with regard to the scandalous precedent of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) in his scurrilous attack on the Public Service of Canada. In light of the fact that cabinet as a whole knew and approved the LRPA purchase contract despite a significant shortfall on November 27, 1975, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather):
That this House deplore the recent attack upon the integrity of the Public Service of Canada made by the Minister of Supply and Services and direct the cabinet to publicly assume the entire responsibility for the failure of the LRPA contract, as both honour and precedent dictate.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RESPONSIBILITY OF FORCE FOR BREAK-IN AT QUEBEC NEWSPAPER OFFICE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, with reference to the policies and responsibilities of the RCMP and the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Allmand), and in particular the report of the RCMP investigation into the break-in at the offices of the Agence de Presse Libre du Quebec. On several occasions this year the Solicitor General has detailed in Hansard his promises to report to the House on this matter. On May 18, as reported on page 13613 of Hansard, he stated he had received a full report from the RCMP but indicated he agreed to let the Quebec solicitor general deal directly with the RCMP, to determine whether something illegal had taken place. That the Solicitor General, as minister responsible for the RCMP, make a statement on motions outlining fully the circumstances and the responsibility for the apparently illegal break and entry into the premises of this Quebec newspaper, above and beyond whatever action the Solicitor General for the province of Quebec intends.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since the new federal government dairy policy was developed because of an alleged overproduction of dairy products, and since the findings of research made in some dairy warehouses, especially for powdered milk, where stocks are equivalent to only 15 days of production, show that those same warehouses are 15 to 20 per cent full, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin):
That simultaneously and without notice, the Standing Committee on Agriculture visit all dairy warehouses to check and make the inventory of existing stocks so that farmers not be penalized for a surplus production which is apparently nonexisting.

speechtext: Does the Minister of National Defence deny the suggestion made by his colleague yesterday that the prime and exclusive responsibility in this matter-I emphasize the word "exclusive"-lies with the customer department, that is to say, with the Minister of National Defence and that none of the responsibility is shared with the Minister of Supply and Services? subsubtopic: LOCKHEED CONTRACT-ACCEPTANCE OF RESPONSIBILITY BY MINISTER AND RECOMMENDATION TO CABINET
speechtext:
I was not in the House yesterday and I am not aware of all that was said yesterday. I can only repeat that the total funding is the responsibility of the user department. National Defence had within its budget $953 million to purchase aircraft and in addition it had approval from the government for more than $100 million for interest payments. The program was funded by National Defence but it was not funded in the years in which payments were required in order to get the most cost effective arrangement with the Lockheed Company. The negotiation of the contract is very definitely not the responsibility of the Department of National Defence. That situation of divided responsibility has existed for many years. I have been Minister of Supply and Services and Minister of National Defence and I understand the distinction and the responsibilities that rest in each of those departments.
I am not at this time wishing to place blame; I am simply trying to answer clearly the question of the Leader of the Opposition. I would think the crucial point in these negotiations turns around the telex that was sent on December 2. It was signed by my colleague the Minister of Supply and Services, but I would share with him, and my officials I believe should share with his officials, responsibility for the sending of that telegram. Because at that time the telegram was sent in the belief that it was in the best interests of the government and the people of Canada, since we were protecting our rights, our price, our industrial benefits and the schedule that had been negotiated over many months. So, I would support the Minister of Supply and Services in the signing of that crucial document.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope I have a question for the Minister of Supply and Services. I would like to know what the minister meant when he gave me that answer last Tuesday about the telegram. In particular, having said in the House yesterday that neither he nor the Minister of Defence on December 2 knew of the details of the financial arrangements that were being worked out with the Lockheed Corporation, then under those circumstances why in heaven's name was that telegram sent on December 2?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
subsubtopic: LOCKHEED CONTRACT-REASON FOR SENDING TELEX ON DECEMBER 2

Mr. Speaker, it is quite simple. If the hon. member refers to what was said in the House and if he wants to use his brains, he will easily understand. As the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) indicated, the deadline to sign an agreement with Lockheed to protect the cost and industrial benefits offered by that company as well as the delivery schedule was December 2. Indeed, on that date, the government sent a telex to Lockheed indicating our desire to negotiate a contract with that company.
Of course, the government was then considering how to meet its financial commitments, as shown by the agreements negotiated between the Crown and Lockheed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Arising out of the statement yesterday by the Minister of Supply and Services in which he said that neither he nor his deputy minister were informed of the financial negotiations by the Department of National Defence and Lockheed prior to December 2, I want to ask the Minister of National Defence if he was aware of the financial negotiations which were going on, and if he was did he at any time pass this information on to the Minister of Supply and Services? speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: LOCKHEED CONTRACT-KNOWLEDGE OF MINISTER OF FINANCIAL NEGOTIATIONS-INFORMATION GIVEN CABINET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it will help the House and the hon. member if I try to make a distinction between the shortfall and Lockheed's inability to finance the shortfall. The shortfall is the difference between the funds that were available in the Department of National Defence and the funds required for payments by Lockheed. That was clearly known in November and it was in the cabinet documents. I have described many times, before the committee and in other ways, that the government approved $100 million in interest for financing. If you are going to have interest for financing, you must be intending to borrow. If you are going to borrow, there must be a shortfall-that is self-evident. So that any number of cabinet ministers who attended those meetings knew there was a shortfall-that is clear.
The timing of Lockheed's inability to provide the interim financing may not be so clear. That was not known to me or to my colleagues until at least mid-December because Lockheed only told us then after the cabinet decision that they could not provide the financing. If anyone has misled anybody in these days it was Lockheed which misled us by saying they could provide the interim financ-


ing. It was not known to me until I returned from the NATO meeting in Brussels that they could not do so. I remember very well coming back here on about December 15 at which time my deputy minister told me for the first time that Lockheed were not able to do what they had said they could do. If that is what my colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services, is referring to, I would like the House to understand the difference. It is one thing to know about the shortfall-which I think we all knew about-and it is another thing to know about Lockheed's failure to provide interim financing, which came at a later date.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like in my remarks today to provide further information regarding the budget announcement relating to employment matters, to deal with some of the unfounded criticisms which have been raised, and to outline the government's views regarding an employment strategy for Canada. I will try to condense my remarks into the 30-minute period allotted, but may need to ask the indulgence of the House for a few minutes of extra time.
May I put the employment aspects of the budget in context by reminding hon. members that the June, 1975, budget announced a two-year program of expanded manpower activities. We are currently in the second year of that program and our regular manpower budgets are being augmented as follows: first, there is a $40 million increase in institutional and industrial training bringing the total available for training in the fiscal 1976-77 to $522 million, and enabling the training this fiscal year of over 305,000 Canadians; second, there is an additional $2 million for our mobility program, expanding our budget in 1976-77 to $13.7 million. This enables us to undertake the permanent relocation of 15,000 families, and covers other mobility grants to between 40,000 and 45,000 workers. Next, there is an enrichment of our job finding and placement services, costing an extra $3 million, and involving an additional staff of 150 for our Canada Manpower centres. Finally, there is a $100 million job creation program for next
The Budget-Mr. Andras
winter. It is untrue to say we are doing nothing this year for the unemployed.
We are continuing to analyse the labour market prospects and are carefully considering whether additional funds should or could be provided. In the meantime, plans are proceeding, based on the approved level of financing. I shall announce the details of the 1976-77 Local Initiatives Program in a few days.
While not minimizing the seriousness of the situation during the present fiscal year, 1976-77, I should like to focus my remarks today primarily on the longer term employment problems and prospects of our country for 1977 through to 1981.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where is your crystal ball?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am about to look into it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I cannot see it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Our best estimate is that labour force growth will be somewhat less over the next five years than it was in the past ten years, but I caution that labour force forecasts are extremely hazardous. We know fairly well how many youths will come into the labour market each year and we know how many workers will retire or die. We can and we will control immigration. However, we cannot accurately forecast what will happen to participation rates. Moreover, we know that while we have a labour force of about ten million people at any given time, there are actually closer to 13 million Canadians who work during the year, and almost five million job changes. How many of these part-time or intermittent workers will become or even want to become full-time regular employees, we just cannot tell with precision, but we can make some rough forecasts based on certain assumptions.
First, we are assuming a somewhat slower growth in participation rates than over the past few years. We are also assuming a reduction in immigration from a gross level of about 200,000 in the last two years to under 150,000. With these assumptions, we forecast labour force growth at from 1.1 million to 1.2 million over the next five years.
We also forecast that employment growth will exceed labour force growth by about 100,000. That will bring unemployment down only gradually. That is of great concern to us, and the government is therefore committed to reducing-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that five years?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1977 through 1981, five years, yes. The government is committed to reducing this unacceptable level of unemployment by direct job creation and other measures which I will outline today, and in more detail in the fall session.
Our goal is not necessarily a 5 V4 per cent or even 5 per cent unemployment rate. Our goal is the fullest employment rate possible in light of inflationary pressures and the international economic situation. It must be realized, as the Economic Council of Canada recently pointed out, that unemployment in Canada is not as simple or as comprehensible as it once was. There is an over-all shortage of
9SS68-S7V2


The Budget-Mr. Andras
jobs, but a significant proportion of current unemployment is caused by structural problems, problems such as the particular difficulties of youth, of women, of native peoples, the handicapped, or regional economic disparities, and skill mismatches.
Some unemployment, which we call frictional unemployment, results from the sheer dynamism of the labour market which even in the best of economic times always has some people between jobs. Some other unemployment is the effect of our lessening but still significant seasonal labour market fluctuations.
We analysed the available data. We concluded that the 1975 unemployment rate of about 7 per cent was composed roughly of four percentage points of frictional and structural unemployment, 2.7 percentage points of cyclical unemployment, and about .3 per cent of seasonal unemployment. We therefore see that over half of our unemployment is due to frictional and structural causes. This situation simply cannot be solved by any one program or policy nor by simplistic generalized solution. It requires an array of more fully developed and precisely aimed manpower programs focusing specifically on each element of the unemployment total.
It is clear that we must improve and expand our policy and programs to create jobs, to provide occupational training and mobility, to help the disadvantaged and the handicapped and to help young people bridge the growing gap between school and work. We have been developing comprehensive and effective manpower programs and services, but let's face the fact that, frankly, the costs are enormous.
It takes about $200 million to shave less than one quarter of a percentage point from our unemployment rate for a full year by putting the unemployed into training or job creation projects.
To reduce our current unemployment to 5 per cent would cost about $2 billion more per year using training, and a local initiatives type program which is by far the cheapest available to government.
We have scoured the world and we have concluded that the best job creation approach is one which does the following: first, expands the stock of regular jobs in the private sector as much as possible without generating a new round of inflation; second, maximizes our utilization of existing jobs by improved manpower services, mobility and training, and by a tighter control of immigration.
We are doing all these things, and in 1976 we shall receive 40,000 to 50,000 fewer immigrants than in 1975, and tighten up our issuance of employment visas to temporary workers.

speechtext:
It is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said. I heard him last night. I say that in spite of the lead story of the CBC. I suggest that the hon. member obtain a transcript before making any further comments.
Third, we want a plan that creates as many jobs by direct job creation programs as we can afford, at the lowest possible overhead cost, and with the least possible disruption of the regular private sector labour market.

We need resources to do the job. We need money. We also need a new policy approach and employment strategy. Our labour market is too dynamic and our problems too complex and fluid to be able to afford a fragmented, inefficient approach to employment policy and to the organization of the labour market.
That is why we are merging the UIC and the Department of Manpower and Immigration into the new Commission and Department of Employment and Immigration, and that is why I propose that the new organization should benefit from the continued and strengthened participation of business and labour in its work, both at the national policy level and at the local operational level. I shall have more to say about this when I introduce a bill in the next session of parliament to authorize the integration.
For the same reason I feel strongly that the activities of all levels of government in the labour market must be better co-ordinated. I have recently met with my provincial colleagues and we are unanimously agreed on this point. We plan to meet early in the fall to deal with a number of major issues involving not only the effectiveness of federal efforts and plans, but also such matters as the growing concern about the lack of effective linkage between the worlds of school and work which contributes to our high unemployment among youth in Canada.
With this strong institutional base, and co-operation with the private sector and between governments, we can reduce our employment problems in Canada if we can find the resources to do so, and I shall try to explain how resources might be made available.
I have long been concerned about the anomaly in Canada of substantial numbers of unemployed people receiving income maintenance on the one hand while there is a great deal of public work and training which needs to be done, and a shortage of public funds to do it. For that reason, I have proposed an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act which will allow the government to develop programs whereby Canadians who are in receipt of unemployment insurance can participate in public employment programs and occupational training.
The principle underlying this proposal is that unemployment is costly not only for our economy and society but most particularly for the worker who loses his or her job. Idleness brings loss of skills and of confidence, and erodes the worker's feeling of participating in his community. While he needs, and has a right to, income maintenance, we would like to be able to offer him something more.
We are now developing job creation models in which workers who are likely to be unemployed and on unemployment insurance for some months would be invited to participate in activities of social value for the betterment of their communities. We have in mind projects which could utilize many of the best features of earlier Local Initiatives Programs but which could be tailored more carefully to the needs of the individual and the community. There could be included arrangements for the individual to spend some time in a continued job search and in job counselling.
Our plan would be to have participants continue to receive U.I. benefits and we would provide other moneys,


for example, for cost of work allowances and project overhead costs, from additional moneys which would have to be voted for this purpose.
Some people are repeatedly on unemployment insurance because they lack basic job skills and they would benefit from occupational training or retraining. There is already some integration of unemployment insurance and training allowances but the system is complex, and unfortunately the training program cannot accommodate all who need training. We have been experimenting in Newfoundland with a pilot stfheme to use unemployment insurance more productively in financing training, and our experience to date warrants expansion of such projects.
Another potential developmental use of unemployment insurance is the short work week. A well-established system in Europe enables enterprises which propose to lay off part of their work force to retain all workers on the job but on shorter hours, with allowances being paid in respect of the difference between the hours worked and the normal work week. Naturally it would require the co-operation and agreement of both company and union, and initially it would be done on a very selective basis. It has the great advantage of maintaining job attachment and skills of workers during temporary business downturns.
Other aspects of the unemployment insurance program also require change, primarily for reasons of equity and to promote a more effective labour market. In the course of our comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program we have identified certain categories of workers for whom present coverage can be regarded as inappropriate.
The efficiencies and savings in the unemployment insurance program which we will be able to achieve if parliament approves our proposed changes will provide us with additional resources to devote to the prevention and alleviation of unemployment-and that is how we intend to use those resources. Mr. Speaker, Canada has one of the most efficient and comprehensive unemployment insurance programs in the world, but it must constantly be adapted to meet changes in society and in the labour market. The proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act announced in the budget are designed to make that program more effective in protecting Canadian workers from the economic impact of unemployment, without in the process unnecessarily spending money which would be better allocated to employment programs.
During our comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program we devoted particular attention to the benefit structure which in many respects is the core of the legislation. Based on our own analyses and the advice and comments we have received from many private organizations and individuals, we reached the conclusion that a recasting of the benefit structure is now in order.
The proposals we have in mind are designed to enhance motivation to work, to achieve a greater degree of simplicity, and to provide more equity. A greater degree of simplicity will be obtained by reducing the number of phases from the present five to three. There will be a more equitable relationship between the number of insured weeks and benefit entitlement in the initial benefit period. Greater equity will result from eliminating the national unemployment rate as a trigger for extended benefits, and basing
The Budget-Mr. Andras
regional extended benefits entirely on regional unemployment rates which are a better indication of the difficulty of obtaining and retaining employment.
While the benefit entitlement of those with a shorter labour force attachment will in general be curtailed, adequate income protection will continue to be provided for those with longer labour force attachment and for those residing in regions with high unemployment rates.
In summary, the benefit structure based on three phases of initial phase, labour force attachment phase, and regionally extended benefits phase will be designed to provide continuing adequate income replacement during periods, and in regions of high unemployment, but will result in curtailed benefits and reduced costs at lower rates of unemployment.
We also propose to increase the minimum entrance requirement for the unemployment insurance program from eight to 12 insured weeks. The purpose of this amendment is to bring unemployment insurance more in line with realistic principles of social insurance programs and with the realities of the labour market. The Canadian unemployment insurance program now ranks among the best and most generous in the world. At eight weeks our entrance requirement is the most generous in the world, and we will still be among the most generous national schemes at 12 weeks. Since the announcement of this proposal I have been gratified by the reaction in the Canadian press and from many people in both the private and public sectors.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The alleged impact of our proposal has been denounced as tampering with a very fine unemployment insurance program at a time of high unemployment, and simply shifting the burden of cost on to the provinces. These critics have based their statements on a complete misunderstanding of the facts of the situation, which I would like to clarify.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Talk to Mackasey and Herb Breau.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Reference has been made to a figure of
330,000	individuals who would be affected by the increased entrance requirement. It is essential to interpret this figure correctly. It is an estimate of the total number of individuals who, on the basis of eight to 11 weeks of insured earnings, would receive benefits during the whole of 1976 at an unemployment rate of 7 per cent. This does not mean, as has been alleged by many commentators, that


The Budget-Mr. Andras
at any moment of time in the year 330,000 people would be affected. Because the average duration of benefits extends only for a portion of the year-17 weeks-at any moment in time only about 100,000 individuals would be affected. It is nonsense and irresponsible to argue that all of these individuals will, as a result of a higher entrance requirement, be prevented from receiving benefits and will be, in fact, taken off the unemployment insurance rolls.
Based on our analysis of the work behaviour patterns of the "eight to 11 weekers," we have estimated that a substantial number of them, indeed between 40 and 50 per cent, will be able immediately or within the qualifying period to work for the additional four weeks and thereby qualify at the higher entrance requirement. This in fact means that at any moment of time only abo it 50,000 individuals nationally would not be able to receive benefits.
Particular concern has been expressed about the Atlantic provinces where employment conditions are less favourable. In these provinces we estimate that at any point in time only 10,000 individuals would not be able immediately to find 12 weeks of insured earnings.
In order to assess the impact of the higher entrance requirement on the 50,000 individuals in Canada as a whole, or the 10,000 individuals in the Atlantic provinces, it is essential to bear the fundamental characteristics of those individuals in mind. The overwhelming majority of them,.indeed about 80 per cent, have no dependants. This would mean that of those excluded from benefits at any point in time, only 10,000 individuals in Canada as a whole, or 2,000 people in the Atlantic provinces, would have dependants.
Moreover, the eight to 11 weekers, as we call them, are approximately four years younger on average than the remainder of the claimants. Almost half of them are under 25 years of age. Many of the eight to 11 weekers are in fact secondary earners, such as working wives and young persons living at home. They are members of families who already have a main breadwinner. Studies have shown that in many cases these families have incomes in the middle and higher ranges.
As a result of this analysis, Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that very few of the eight to 11 weekers will find it necessary to turn to welfare. Moreover, it is our intention to direct our developmental programs of training and job creation to those individuals and areas requiring assistance to establish more stable employment patterns.
Furthermore, I want to make the point that a study of 1974 claimants found that 64 per cent of the group with eight to 11 weeks' attachment at that time had dropped out of the labour force one year later, by March, 1975. We did not know these facts before; these figures have all come out of the recent analysis. Many of these people subsequently re-entered the labour force and worked for a sufficiently long period of time to establish another unemployment insurance claim. In other words, many of this group are particularly prone to move in and out of the labour force, in and out of jobs, on and off claim, and apparently suffer little or no hardship.

Contrary to the popular impression, Mr. Speaker, seasonal employment patterns are not the prime cause. Only 30 per cent of the eight to 11 weekers have established a seasonal type repeat pattern. This compares with 43 per cent for those with major labour force attachments. Our belief that claimants with eight to 11 weeks of insured employment have little difficulty moving in and out of the labour force has been reinforced by other statistics. For example, eight to 11 weekers have a greater tendency to draw down their full entitlement under the act than the claimants with 12 or more weeks of insured employment. However, we cannot really conclude from this that things are tougher for them; quite the contrary. A 1973 survey showed that 70 per cent of all eight to 11 weekers have found work within six weeks of exhausting their benefits. And what happened to the remaining claimants who did not find a job after six weeks? This is the welfare question.
Despite the fact that of all UI claimants, exhaustees could be assumed to be the most needy-"exhaustees" are those people who have run out their full entitlement-it was found that only 8 per cent of exhaustees resorted to welfare, or less than 2 per cent of the total unemployment insurance claimants.
These figures may be taken as an indication of two things. First, eight to 11 weekers who want or need to take another job tend to find one very quickly once UI benefits are no longer available. Secondly, many of those who do not find a job do not do so because they were not seriously tied to the labour force in the first place.
Some critics have pointed to the fact that eight to 11 weekers tend to be low wage earners, and that is quite true. But these claimants usually have no dependants, as I have indicated; they are usually young, mobile, and generally more successful in finding new employment, and are often secondary workers and members of middle to higher income families. I think that places the fact that they are also low wage earners in an entirely different perspective.
Critics have said that this proposal for a 12 week entrance requirement will hurt the Atlantic provinces or hurt Quebec. I can assure hon. members from high unemployment areas that we will tilt our expanded manpower programs and services so that the unemployed in those areas will not suffer financially from this change but in fact will gain from the productive impact of these enhanced programs.
What is the effect on the cost of the unemployment insurance program of providing coverage to a group with such an unstable and marginal attachment to the labour force, a group which can move in and out of employment and in and out of the labour market, suffering little economic consequence? This is the effect, Mr. Speaker. The cost ratio of claimants with eight to 11 insured weeks is 20 times the ratio for the average claimant. I believe that this money could be better spent. I believe that priority and funding should go to programs which deal more directly with the underlying problems of the labour market.
It is and always has been one of the primary concerns and purposes of the unemployment insurance program to help workers maintain a steady, constant connection with the labour market. In retrospect, Mr. Speaker, now we have the experience and the analysis of five to six years under our belt, I think that the eight week entrance


requirement has not been successful in furthering this goal and in fact has created a disincentive in the labour market.
I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that there may be some genuine hardship for a few in this group. In order to keep off welfare any eight to 11 weekers who are in genuine difficulty in finding and keeping steady employment, surely it would be much more appropriate to develop and strengthen special job creation, job counselling, and mobility programs targeted to specific groups and specific areas, and tailored to suit the needs of youth and marginal atta-chees to the work force. These new or expanded programs will, in my opinion, give the right kind of help to any eight to 11 weeker who really needs help.
It should also be stressed that even with the higher number of weeks of insured employment, Canada's entrance requirement for unemployment insurance will remain, apart from The Netherlands, the most generous of any industrialized country in the world. For example, Sweden's entrance requirement is based on 12 months of contributions, five being within the last year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This package of proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act will also bring about a change in the severance pay provision. The existing UI regulations treat severance pay as earnings for the purpose of unemployment insurance benefits. We have examined this and I feel that there is a very good reason to treat severance pay as a form of deferred savings which are accumulated during the period of employment.
The fact is that many employers and unions are able to work out mutually satisfactory arrangements for the purpose of getting around that existing regulation, so I think it should be revoked. Other amendments are designed to increase the incentive to work, for example, with respect to the so-called "four week rule". This rule now means that an individual who does not receive extended benefits for four weeks or more has his claim permanently terminated. Experience has indicated that this rule has clearly served as a deterrent for claimants to return to short-term work that last longer than four weeks, so therefore we propose to eliminate it.
They are the major changes that I propose to make in the unemployment insurance program at this time. The primary purpose of the changes is to promote a more equitable and effective labour market and to free funds for more productive use in job creation and training. With these
The Budget-Mr. Andras
funds, and the potential flexibility offered by the other amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, I expect to be able to recommend to my colleagues an employment strategy for the years ahead which would include these elements: a new, year-round, multi-faceted, direct job creation program which would build on the successes of earlier Local Initiative Programs; take account of the proposals of the Economic Council and others; and attack cyclical, seasonal, area-specific, and, to some extent, structural unemployment, in ways tailored to local needs and targeted to areas and groups suffering high unemployment.
For example, unemployed heads of families not eligible for unemployment insurance would be given a special priority in entry to this program, which would include a creative linkage of all labour market programs, particularly the more productive use of unemployment insurance in developmental activities; a strategy for youth employment covering not only student summer employment but the more serious and pervasive problems of unemployed school dropouts and graduates; it would require expanded training and mobility programs, and other employment policies which respond to the needs of particular groups of workers and employers, and which support economic and manpower adjustments and productivity improvement.
I have outlined today a number of legal and institutional changes which will facilitate, in my opinion and in the opinion of the government, a more effective employment policy in this country. I will be announcing details of that policy in the months to come, and in the meantime I truly invite hon. members' ideas and suggestions and will welcome them. This is going to require a lot of work and it will be a difficult exercise with all the interfaces we have to examine. I must emphasize again that we need amendments to legislation to give effect to this policy and to secure the necessary financial resources.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as it was recognized by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in his budget presentation, and again by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) this afternoon, that there is recognition under these new proposals of the benefit structure with regard to the regional unemployment situation, for which I commend the minister, I wonder whether he can give some indication, since the qualification period is to be raised from eight weeks to 12 weeks-at the present time the figures I have looked at show that those who would fall most heavily in that group are in areas of chronic high unemployment, plus areas which have industries which are largely seasonal; I think for instance of the major industries in the Atlantic provinces such as fisheries, tourism, and agriculture, which by their very nature offer short-term employment, in fact even less than the new 12-week qualification period proposed by the minister-of any definite plan he has in mind in respect to flexibility in this area? Or can he offer any particular guarantee that the people who are available for employment, but because of their attachment to seasonal industry will simply not be able to obtain employment, will have a definite commitment of employment other than simply moving from unemployment insurance benefits to welfare?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Mr. Speaker, the elements of the job creation plan, first of all, will be very definitely tilted, that is, weighted through funding and application, to those various high unemployment areas, and indeed Atlantic Canada

is unfortunately one of them. In terms of the decision or the guarantee the hon. member is asking for, I would like to examine that as we work it out. I tell you frankly that there are a great number of things that we still have to put together, which will be in the next two or three months, and I hope I will be in a position to come to parliament in the fall to give then details of a more precise application to local situations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One supplementary question, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry, but there will be lots of time for questions later on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Vancouver on Monday the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was in one of his philosophical moods. He said at that time that only "a conspiracy of love" can save mankind. That is what the philosopher, Pierre, is reported as having said. Well, talk is cheap. Such hypocrisy, to put it in its coldest terms, simply cannot be ignored. The only tangible evidence of a conspiracy as it is influencing the Government of Canada now is not one of love. On the contrary, it is directed at Canadian men and women among those most in need in our country. It is a conspiracy, in short, against the unemployed in Canada, and nothing the minister has said this afternoon, and I propose to deal in some detail with what he has said, has caused me to change my judgment on this issue one iota.
The minister said, just picking up a couple of details at the outset, that it was wrong for critics to allege that
330,000	Canadians are going to be affected as a result of the announced changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. He said it is very misleading, and that only 100,000 at any one time will be affected; that the 330,000 are spread throughout the year. Presumably those 100,000 people are to take some consolation from that fact. He said also that at any one time only 10,000 of those affected by the change from the eight weeks to the 12 weeks happen to reside in Atlantic Canada. Again I say to you, that is some solace to the 10,000 involved in Atlantic Canada.
It is almost impossible to imagine a more calculatingly cruel budget than the one the minister brought down last week. It has been said that the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has simply neglected Canada's unemployed. I emphatically disagree with that. He has consciously brought in a budget which, at every crucial point, touches directly those thousands of men and women in every part of Canada who find themselves unable to obtain jobs.
Let us first consider the tax policy. What was required in this budget was a tax cut for middle and low income families in order to stimulate an economy in which manufacturing is running at only 80 per cent capacity. Instead, the minister brought forward tax benefits for upper income Canadians who alone have disposable income at home, enabling them to invest more lavishly in registered retirement savings plans. Without the needed stimulus which tax cuts would have provided, the cruel result will be increased unemployment, and the minister knows it.


Second, in respect of fiscal policy, the minister has announced that he plans to reduce the deficit by a further $900 million at a time when there are more than 760,000 Canadian out of work. Such a step inevitably means fewer, not more jobs. Again I say the minister knows it, and knows it very well.
Third, finally and most brutally of all, the two major changes proposed in the Unemployment Insurance Act will mean a direct increase in the misery of our unemployed. There is no other conclusion that a fair-minded person could draw who knows the implications of the changes which would cut 330,000 people entirely off from benefits and which would reduce substantially the benefits of those who need them most, namely, those Canadian men and women in areas where regional unemployment is most persistent. The minister has attacked precisely those in Canada who are in greatest need.
Unlike certain commentators I do not regard the minister as he has been described in certain quotations recently. I do not describe him as tough-minded, or courageous, or practical, when he takes such a stand as revealed in this budget. Quite the contrary. I regard him as being politically cynical and chillingly smug. Who, I ask, is tough-minded when he kicks people who are down? Who is courageous when he yields to widespread indifference about the poor and the unemployed in Canada? Where is the political leadership which cashes in on the sad sentiment that our unemployed are responsible for their own misfortune?
In my comments today I want to show not only that the budget proposals are morally offensive, which they are, but that they are wrong from a purely technical point of view as to what it is possible to achieve now in 1976 in our economy. For if it is wrong to be cruel when it is possible to be magnanimous, it is equally wrong in politics to pretend that more justice should be done if it is impossible to do so. Hypocrisy, I say, cannot be a substitute for callousness.
Let me dwell specifically now on the changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act because I think, and my colleagues and this party think, and all kinds of sensitive people from one coast to another coast in Canada think, this is the most reprehensible aspect of the budget. A myth is abroad in the country. The myth is that we are in substantial debt in the unemployment insurance program, that somehow the taxpayers are being forced to make up this debt. Well, the reality is that the largest part of the program, that which is the direct responsibility of working Canadians and employers, has a substantial surplus. There is no debt at all. The surplus for last year was in the range of $400 million, and in the current year it is estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $200 million. This means that the working men and women of our country are fully paying their share of a program that was set up for their benefit. They are not, in respect of the overwhelming number of dollars being spent on the program, being subsidized by anyone. They are paying through an insurance scheme for their own benefits.
At present, unemployment insurance costs beyond the 5.4 per cent unemployment level are paid for by the federal government out of the federal treasury. The justification for this is that unemployment of such magnitude-and it is
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
one of the worst of all the industrial countries of the world-is not by any conceivable line of reasoning the responsibility of the men and women who have to suffer its ravages. Rather it is the collective responsibility of all of us in this country, and in particular it is the responsibility of the federal Government of Canada whose obligation it is to manage the economy in a way in which jobs are available for everyone who wants to work. That is the first myth.
The second myth-and we have all heard this-is that there are plenty of jobs available for all those who want to get out and look for them. I am sure every member of parliament regardless of the party to which he belongs can cite stories about meeting people in his constituency office, or about meeting people in subways and on airlines, who come to him and say that if people want to get out and find a job they can find one.
What is the reality in 1976? The fact is that there are now more than 12 men and women in Canada available for every job that is open. There are more than 12 men and women available for every job from Vancouver to St. John's. What this cruel statistic means is that if every available job were taken up tomorrow there would remain in our country more than 700,000 Canadians who want to work, who are desirous of getting out and contributing to our economy, who do not want unemployment insurance benefits, who do not want welfare, but who want to make their contribution and are unable to find a job. That is the reality.
The New Democratic Party says that the only acceptable, sensible, and relevant way to bring down the cost of unemployment insurance in Canada is for the Government of Canada to manage its economy in such a way that jobs are available. That, Mr. Speaker, is precisely to what last week's budget should have addressed itself. Instead of taking aim at the problems of the unemployed, the budget brought in by the new minister took aim at the unemployed themselves.
Let us consider in a fair-minded way, but I hope with some sense of compassion, the two major changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act that were announced in the budget. First, the government plans to change the five-phase structure of benefits to a three-phase one, contending that this will help those in areas of persistently high unemployment. The minister in his remarks earlier this afternoon repeated the argument. Mr. Speaker, I say to that: what a cruel hoax, because a hoax it is. It is the case that some people will benefit from this particular change, but I will illustrate to you why, particularly for Canadians in Atlantic Canada, in Quebec, in northern Ontario and in southeastern Ontario, the change is, as I say, a cruel hoax that will mean disadvantages for those people, not advantages.
More often than not people in the areas I have just listed will suffer more, not less. Consider a man or woman in the province of Nova Scotia who has had 20 weeks of insured earnings, that is, he or she has been working and productive in the Canadian community for at least five months, and he or she finds himself or herself laid off for whatever reason. Under the present law such a person would be entitled to up to 51 weeks of benefits. I want to stress the entitlement to up to 51 weeks. Most such people are active-
14092


The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
ly seeking employment, and if they are not they are cut off from benefits. People in our country who are fully employed have to be reminded of the fact that if the unemployed are not actively seeking a job, they are cut off.
I come back to the particular case of a man or woman who has worked for five months, is out of work, is in Nova Scotia and is trying to find employment. That person is trying to bring in money for a family at home. Under the present law that person can claim benefits for up to 51 weeks if he or she is unable to find a job. But under the proposed changes that the minister so glowingly referred to this afternoon, that same person would be entitled to at most 40 weeks of benefits-a reduction of some 20 per cent in the time of benefits to which that person is entitled. The New Democratic Party says, shame to that, and shame on a government that brings in a scheme that has this kind of effect on people in Canada who need more, not less, assistance.
Consider another person in the same province of Nova Scotia, this time one with 12 weeks of insured earnings. Under the present scheme such a man or woman could get up to 44 weeks of benefits, again I repeat, assuming they are actively seeking employment. Under the budget proposals announced by the Minister of Finance last Tuesday and reiterated here this afternoon by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), instead of getting up to 44 weeks of benefits that person would have a maximum of 32 weeks. This means a drop in the number of weeks of benefits by more than 25 per cent for a man or woman in Nova Scotia who happens to be in that particular situation.
The point I am making is that at a time when we have the highest level of unemployment in our country in 15 years, in a part of Canada where unemployment is even higher than the average, the government's change is one which cruelly hits at those most in need of benefits. Although I refer in my examples to Nova Scotia, it goes without saying that I could have selected New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, or whole regions in the province of Quebec. The same persistently high level of unemployment exists in all these parts of Canada. In all these parts of Canada these negative results will follow from changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Consider also the effects of extending the minimum employment period for any benefits from eight weeks to 12 weeks. Once again those parts of the country which need assistance most will be treated first. It is precisely in Atlantic Canada and in many parts of Quebec that seasonal or short run jobs are the principal source of income.
The hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) was questioning the minister earlier this afternoon and very correctly pointed out that workers in those parts of Canada compared to the rest of the people in our country are disproportionately employed in the fisheries, in tourism, and in agriculture. And he was quite correct in the implication of his question that the people who will be most negatively affected by this cruel change from eight weeks to 12 weeks are precisely the same people. The fact is that people employed in these occupations very frequently cannot get a job that lasts longer than eight weeks.

That is the cold reality, and members in the House from Atlantic Canada and from the province of Quebec know that very well. Now that such people will no longer be eligible for unemployment insurance after working up to 11 weeks, the municipalities of Saint John, New Brunswick; St. John's, Newfoundland; Halifax, Nova Scotia, and Rouyn, Quebec, will be paying increased welfare costs.
I do not care what the minister said earlier today because the men and women who will not be able to work and to get the benefits that they were once getting, will need financial resources in order to feed their families, and at least in Canada we have reached the point where we will not permit people to starve. If we will not permit people to starve, it means that the cities in these areas will pay increased welfare costs for these people, and it means indirectly of course that the provincial governments in these areas will have to pick up a major part of the tab for the increased welfare costs.
Is it any wonder that every premier in every province in Atlantic Canada is opposed to these measures? Is it any wonder that any informed Canadian, no matter where he may live, with an ounce of moral conscience, who knows the facts about the implications of this proposed change, is disgusted with the whole thrust of the budget?
The minister this afternoon said he would be interested in providing more information about the discussions that have taken place between his government and the governments in Atlantic Canada. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I have been in touch with most of the premiers of the provinces in Atlantic Canada and, without exception, they are fundamentally and totally opposed to this legislation. They are opposed to this legislation because they know it is cruel and callous and because their provincial treasuries, which are already hard pressed compared to the more affluent parts of Canada, will have to pick up the tab.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why, one must ask, is this Liberal government doing what it is doing? I will offer a theory on what the Liberal Party of Canada in 1976 is up to. They are simply yielding to the concern-and I put that in italics- about unemployment abuses about which we have all heard. However, they are concerned not about Canada in general but mainly about the province of Ontario because they know that when the next election comes in 1978- assuming their relatively safe base in the province of Quebec-it will be the cities in Ontario that will elect most members to the House of Commons. I put forward for hon. members consideration that the kind of callous disregard that is being expressed in this budget and in these changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act is designed to appease the indifference in part and in part the legitimate concern with unemployment insurance of people in the mote affluent province of Ontario. Instead of supporting these changes, we in this party are in favour of enforcing the existing law. We are in favour of getting at those who cheat this system, or cheat any other laws on the books of Canada.
Instead of dealing directly with these abuses, what the government has brought forward are these two major amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which would deal with the sentiment that is expressed in the big


cities of affluent Ontario but has, as its effect, a kick in the pants and a little more to the people in Atlantic Canada. That is great disservice to the people of this country. Such a policy is nothing short of despicable. It provokes anger on our part with the government for bringing it in at this time. I would be less than straightforward however, if I said I was not equally concerned with the official position so far put forward on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada.
The official spokesman for the Conservative party said in his initial response to the budget that the one thing he thought the Government of Canada was sensible about in its budget was its announced changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act. The same member has described unemployed Canadians as "lead swingers". He announced this change in this budget as one small step forward. I hope that a number of members in that party from Atlantic Canada who know reality and who, I think, speak honestly for the people they represent, will have some influence with the official opposition when it comes to the vote on our amendment and can bring some sense and some decency to the formation of their position.
I said earlier that it is not enough for a political party to make a moral criticism of a government. If we are going to suggest that a moral alternative is what should be pursued it is also obligatory, to avoid the serious political charge of hypocrisy, to suggest how it might be possible. In the conclusion of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to do precisely that.
As the Minister of Finance well knows, we now have in the Canadian economy a manufacturing sector that is functioning at only 80 per cent capacity. In straightforward economic terms that no economist would deny, this means that we could have had stimulation now, in 1976, by means of a tax cut for people on average and low incomes. This would stimulate the economy and cause manufacturing industries to call men and women who want jobs in off the streets. They would produce the goods that an increased supply of money would demand. And the point is there would not be an iota of new pressure on inflation. That is the crucial point, Mr. Speaker.
On budget night the Minister of Finance said that if we stimulate the economy it will cause inflation. He was only half right or, more correctly, only telling a half truth. If you have an economy that is already functioning at maximum capacity where there is no slack in our offices or factories and you stimulate it, then the minister is right; you cause great inflation. When you are only operating at 80 per cent capacity, however, and when you have more than 760,000 Canadians who want jobs, a tax reduction would cause stimulation and take people off the streets to work, but would not cause any increase in inflation.
The minister took a callous and cynical approach in this budget, Mr. Speaker. He announced forthcoming changes in unemployment insurance which will wreak havoc with many men and women, particularly in Atlantic Canada, who are going to lose the benefits we have built up over a period of time in a fine Unemployment Insurance Act. Beyond that, he did not stimultate the economy in a way that at least during this year could have brought the
The Budget-Mr. Alexander
unemployment level below 7 per cent. Instead, throughout this year unemployment will remain above that grotesque level which no one with any sense of decency in politics finds tolerable.
I urge members in this House to give serious consideration to supporting the amendment put forward by the New Democratic Party which would have the effect of removing that disreputable change. If we had support from members on both sides of the House for the amendment, even though it did not carry, the message of concern that most decent people in the country feel about unemployment might even get through to the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you for recognizing me at this time, Mr. Speaker. I take a very dim view of the minister and his predecessor continually telling us that we should be proud of our most generous unemployment insurance scheme. We do not want a generous unemployment insurance scheme; what we want are jobs. This is the only way we can reduce the significant impact of unemployment insurance-by the creation of jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) will remember the undertaking he gave to me to table the documents, surveys, studies and statistics which allowed him to come to the conclusions urged by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) that certain amendments are necessary to the Unemployment Insurance Act. This is most important in order that we may be as apprised of the situation as is the minister. There are a lot of unanswered questions, and we want to know whether the minister has done his best with this horrendous problem of unemployment insurance.
Our friends on the left want to know whether we will give their motion very serious consideration. We have given it serious consideration, and by necessity we have to vote against it. What the New Democratic Party is attempting to put before the Canadian people is the idea that we should accept unemployment insurance as a way of life. They do not want meaningful amendments to this legislation.
I should like to refer to an editorial in this morning's Globe and Mail, Wednesday, June 2. I do not say this newspaper is the Bible, but I think the statements in the lead editorial mirror the thinking of the vast majority of Canadians. The article pointed out that:
The majority of Canadians don't want a program that encourages people to work for a while with the carrot of months of rest. They don't want a program that discourages mobility in the work force or continuity in the job. They don't want any more of those hilarious stories about good life on the pogey.
What do they want?
The article then makes reference to my friend, the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), but I will ignore that. It continues:
.. . but a good many people want an unemployment program that will be even more sensitive to the needs of individuals and the community at large. A program that will be related more directly to job creating schemes-particularly for workers in the 18 to 25 age bracket-and to the problem regions where high unemployment is chronic.
95S68-58V2


The Budget-Mr. Alexander
This is the gist of the situation. We want amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to bring it, as the minister has indicated, to a social insurance program, while at the same time making sure that those who live within high unemployment areas do not suffer. This is all that people are requesting. They want jobs, whether in the private sector or the government, and I will get into that a little later. What they want is a social insurance program that takes into consideration the needs of those in high unemployment areas.
I was amazed to hear the minister say that an eight week qualification period is a disincentive. I am not going to brag or seek any glory with respect to that, but I should like to refer to the debate on second reading of Bill C-229 in Hansard for April 19, 1971, where I said as rep orted at page 5054:
There are several sections in this bill raising questions of interest and concern and calling for deep consideration, not only by members on this side of the House but by members on the other side. Unemployment insurance programs should maintain a proper balance between providing temporary income maintenance and facilitating reabsorption into productive activity. Therefore, with all due respect to the arguments of the minister, I question whether the reduction of the qualifying period to an eight-week attachment to the labour market is practicable in view of the probable abuses that this will encourage. Further, such a short period of time does not indicate even a strong seasonal attachment to the labour force.
The bill was read the second time, referred to the standing committee, considered in committee, then sent back to the House for consideration at the report stage. On June 10, 1971, as recorded at page 6582 of Hansard, an hon. member-I will tell you shortly which one-moved the following motion:
That Bill C-229, An Act respecting unemployment insurance in Canada, be amended by deleting the word "eight" in paragraph (a) of subclause (2) of clause 17, line 16 at page 11, and substituting the word "twelve".
That Bill C-229, An Act respecting unemployment insurance in Canada, be amended by deleting from Schedule A at page 106, under the column titled "Weeks of insurable employment in qualifying period" in Table 1, the figure "8" in the first entry thereunder and substituting the figure "12".
After proposing those amendments I said, as reported by Hansard at pages 6582 and 6583:
All I can say in conclusion is that I am dismayed by this particular clause, and I am afraid that with all the good intentions the government may have, this clause is open to abuse. It removes the incentive that we are all seeking. It certainly does not enhance personal initiative. So, my two motions are an attempt to make the act more reasonable. What we are trying to do is to allow people to help themselves. I think this is what the government should be doing.
The philosophy of my party is that the government should not move in until it is actually and really required. In other words, the individual should be able to help himself, and this is what I like about our philosophy. Governments should not just look after people from their birth to their death, but we are starting to move in this direction. Whether or not Canadian people can afford this is questionable. But I hope that the minister, as well as my colleagues in the House, will appreciate what 1 am saying. It is not that the Canadian people are lazy. Heavens, no, I would never say that. What I am saying is that when you hold out these enticements, these inducements, these carrots, there is bound to be abuse. I hope that the administration which will be set up will be able to cope with these abuses effectively, because I can foresee problems for the department and for the minister. What he has done, in effect, has been to remove the initiative from people to continue to seek work.

That happened in 1971. I will not take credit for the government's present action. After all, it is my duty to tell the government how to show leadership; it is my duty to suggest policies. It took the government six years to figure out what we figured out in five months. I see the Minister of Finance laughing. Mr. Speaker, the facts speak for themselves. We impressed on the minister in that previous debate that the provisions then being proposed would constitute a disincentive to work. The government disagreed. They said, "No, we do not think so." Now the government admits that those provisions to which we objected are a disincentive to work. Consequently it has proposed the amendments now to come before the House.
Let me refer to another document to show that the government does not keep its promises. Six years ago, in June, 1970, the government produced a white paper on unemployment insurance. On page 18 of that report we find the following words:
... fishermen, who have for the past few years been covered as a total group will now be covered only if they are working for someone else... the self-employed fishermen, however, will be provided for. Income stabilization is imperative in the commercial fisheries, with particular reference to the remote fishing communities, and pending completion of plans being prepared specifically for this purpose, self-employed fishermen will be covered by unemployment insurance.
Why has the promised incomes stabilization plan not been introduced? We have demanded it for the past five or six years. Certain people need that kind of help. I remender the minister saying in the past when we debated this matter, "Don't worry, just pass the bill we are considering and we will bring in an incomes stabilization plan." That happened some time ago; so far we have not heard anything about that plan. No wonder people in the Atlantic provinces are upset.
In his speech the minister spoke of savings he intended to effect, and guaranteed they would not involve hardship for people in our slow growth areas. But when I think of what the government has done with regard to our fishermen, am I supposed to feel happy and pat the minister on the back? I cannot do it. We have been too disappointed.
The minister alluded to certain interesting statistics. Apparently some 22 per cent of all unemployment insurance recipients receive benefits for the full 51 weeks and are known as exhausters. Of these, 8 per cent subsequently go on the welfare rolls and constitute between 1 per cent and 2 per cent of all people on welfare. Contrary to what my friends on my left think, there will not be any massive application to welfare offices. The statistics show it will not happen. Why? The evidence suggests, I think, that other sources of income are available to unemployment insurance recipients. In other words, our work patterns are changing. There may be more than one income earner in a family; therefore one member of a family may work off and on and, when unemployed, collect unemployment insurance.
The minister related other significant facts. He suggested that there are more than ten million people in our labour force, that actually our labour force is about 13 million people strong, but that between two million and three million people intermittently enter and leave the work force. Why, Mr. Speaker? I suggest we must blame the generous provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. We ought to be concerned about those who are not


permanently attached to the labour force. The hard core of ten million people is in the work force to stay. Apparently the minister thinks that his proposed amendments will affect about 300,000 people who are included in the roughly three million people not permanently attached to the work force. Under the proposed amendments they will not get benefits.
The impact of the 1971 UIC revision was made apparent by the Economic Council of Canada study entitled "People and Jobs." I think the minister was waiting for the report to be made public before bringing in necessary amendments. Actually the Economic Council report is a scathing condemnation of the government's policies and attitude to manpower and unemployment insurance. Clearly the government has not kept abreast of the times. The Economic Council of Canada says on page 19 of its report:
The wider coverage and higher benefits introduced into the unemployment insurance program in 1971 have probably had four general effects; some increase in voluntary quits, lay-offs and turnover because of reduction in the cost to individuals of periodic bouts of unemployment and an easing of the responsibilities of employers for lay-offs for sickness or maternity; less incentive for some unemployed individuals to search vigorously for work until the end of their benefit period; an inducement for others outside the labour market to seek work in the knowledge that they could thereby qualify for more generous benefits; and finally, in the larger sense, a selective stimulus to the economy through the transfer of hundreds of millions of dollars to individuals and communities affected by unemployment.
The Economic Council is of the opinion that our existing legislation induces people to join the unemployment rolls and is a disincentive to work. It estimates that present legislation induced between 70,000 and 80,000 people to go on unemployment.
Having said that I must indicate that both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration said that changes will be proposed. The House was told that the weeks during which benefits may be drawn will be related more directly to weeks worked, and that regional benefits will be related more closely to regional unemployment. By saying this the government is showing a certain flexibility. It realizes that we face a chronic situation in the Atlantic provinces, parts of Quebec, and other parts of this country which needs special attention. The government is therefore proposing an amendment which will deal with the matter.
It goes further and says that the act will also be amended to permit the payment of unemployment insurance to beneficiaries on a discretionary basis where they take part in such activities as selected employment training or short time work programs. Clearly the government wants to be flexible. It wants to provide for benefit payments on a discretionary basis. I do not know what that means, but will try to find out. The government realizes that it created tremendous difficulties by ignoring the needs of areas like the Atlantic provinces and will be flexible. Notwithstanding the position we have taken, I say that there is nothing wrong with flexibility which, enshrined in legislation, will determine the period of time benefits may be paid in high unemployment areas, and rightly so.
If the government is so concerned about that, why was not some flexibility given in that eight to 12 week formula in order to relieve the pressures and the problems which
The Budget-Mr. Alexander
the minister has recognized in terms of the flexibility with regard to the extension or length of time for the benefits? I hope the minister will be able to answer that question because in many areas of this country people want to know what flexibility means, and who go this far and not further.
We will have to find out where these regions are, how they are going to be determined, how much saving there will be, where the saving will be directed, and what is meant by payments on a discretionary basis. We do not want any pork barrelling for which this government is famous.
I listened to the minister's speech. I have not yet had a chance to digest it. It was a very important speech with a lot of statistics, plans, and so forth and so on. However, the minister did not give it to us in detail. That is a requirement so that we can know what we can do when the bill comes before the House.
We have to see that our slow growth areas are protected. If the minister cannot give us those matters in detail, we will have to think them. I wonder whether the minister has given us another con job. I do not want to get mean with the minister, but we are used to being conned on unemployment insurance. I do not look at any minister in particular-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Bryce is the only one in the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not intend to mention any names this afternoon. My time is extremely limited. In fact I want to know if I can have a little more time because I have just begun the fight.
I sometimes wonder whether the government has any ideas of its own. During the 1974 election we had an incomes policy in which we discussed wage and price controls. The government said no, you will freeze wages, not prices. After the election the first thing we got was wage and price controls. I think the government is bankrupt in programs.
Another matter disturbs me. When the former leader of the opposition indicated that it was wrong to pay taxes on the inflated dollar, the then minister of finance said that was crazy, they could not do it, it would cost too much. But what do we have now? Relief from that.
When we suggested Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission in order to bring counselling, payment of benefits, and job placement under one roof, the government said no. It also said no to the eight to 12 week period. Now we will have the eight to 12 weeks. What kind of a government is this? Do ministers not have any ideas of their own? They always criticize us for not having any ideas, but every time we turn around they are stealing our ideas. They are the greatest bunch of thieves I have ever seen.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me get back to the unemployment insurance proposed amendments. In 1965 there was the divorce. Why? As the present minister indicates, the government thought that a positive manpower program or policy could best mature if it were allowed to develop

The Budget-Mr. Alexander
independent of an unemployment insurance program. What nonsense. What a costly error that was.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was not an error.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is another smart aleck across the way. If it was not an error, why is it not being continued in separation? It was an error.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was the frustration of error in payments, duplication of documentation, and a complicated system of payments between two bureaucracies. The right hand never knew what the left was doing, and neither did it care.
The Council of the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development called for a balanced development of income maintenance and positive utilization measures which would ensure the earliest possible return to employment. In the past the government has made it easy to get on unemployment but doggone hard to get off. It should be the reverse. I am pleased to see that the minister in his wisdom, with the backing of his officials, has now noted that the former was wrong and the latter is right.
The council implied that it would be preferable to have a one stop program. As a matter of fact the Economic Council of Canada referred to the same sort of one stop program with counselling, payment of benefits, and the placement of jobs all under one roof. The result would bring the two functions into closer harmony. It would reduce the incidence of pauses in unemployment insurance, and the staff should be able to determine how seriously recipients are searching for jobs.
We are all getting a little concerned about the search for jobs. We have seen some significant moves of late. Through the good offices of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration there are now Manpower offices in provincial welfare offices. This enables the matching of people with jobs. There is a feeling that there are too many people seeking welfare as a way of life when there are jobs going begging. I know there are a lot of problems with respect to the atmosphere in which a job may be, the amount of pay, and all the other matters that can make a job a little tough to accept. However, there are a lot of good jobs available. There is now a move in the direction of matching people with jobs in co-operation with the welfare officers and the Ministry of Manpower.
Severance pay is another matter of concern. Two or three years ago the minister not only said he would examine severance pay but holiday pay. I do not know why he is only bringing in severance pay in terms of relief and not holiday pay. There may be a matter of discrimination in this area.
I listened to the minister state something to the effect that unions and business could get together. Is severance pay universal? If the minister is talking about the unionized portion of the labour force, he is only talking about one third. What about the other two thirds? Are they entitled as of right to severance pay? I will have to look into that because I do not want the minister to bring in any bill that is discriminatory and not equitable. If the government is going to move in that direction, why not move in

terms of holiday pay, which I understand through provincial legislation is universal? The minister will have to expand on that.
We are all concerned about jobs. The state of the economy is of major concern to all, particularly the unemployed.
