Here we are faced with the worst of both worlds, high unemployment and high inflation. There are 760,000 people, some 7.4 per cent of the work force, who would like to work but are unemployed. That is the highest for some 15 years. These are heads of families who cannot get jobs and who want to work in order to gain the necessities of life for their families.
The young people who represent the highest incidence of unemployment cannot find jobs. Now we have the students coming on to the labour market. What are we going to do about the students? We have raised this question many times. What is going to happen to some one million students who will be coming out-if they are not already out-and who will add to that total of 750,000 people already unemployed? These people are victims of a mismanaged economy, an inept government which is both callous and cavalier about the plight of its citizens.
The climate is one of concern, despair, and resentment. Imagine the situation. Here we are, a country the envy of most others in terms of wealth-wealth in natural resources, in human resources, wealth in technology-and yet we cannot achieve a 5 per cent real growth level. Is that not amazing? In the period 1974-75 we were short seven percentage points, the equivalent of $7 billion or $330 for every man, woman and child in the country. This is a situation which, in effect, leads to further unemployment.
What is significant, Mr. Speaker, is that for every percentage point of real growth we gain something like 30,000 jobs. So when we are seven points behind we are in effect 200,000 jobs behind. That is why we on this side of the House say the least the Minister of Finance should have done was to give us some indication that he was trying to get something in the region of at least 6 per cent real growth. But no, he is talking about some 4 or 5 per cent, as if that were some big thing. And with every percentage point we lose on real growth we are out some 30,000 jobs. It does not take long to figure that out.
Jobs are a most important consideration in our economy. In this regard the private sector should be and must be the primary source.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When I say that, I do so in the knowledge that this cannot be achieved under the stewardship of the Minister of Finance. I say this because the private sector has no confidence in the government, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) goes around talking about his new society-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And love.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, love is something we heard about the other day. And you know what Mother Theresa said about love. Then again, charity begins at home. But let me not get away from what I have to say. The new society


musings of the Prime Minister, and his light dismissal of the free enterprise and free market system have caused the business community concern. There has been no meaningful restraint on the part of the federal government. It is increasing its expenditures by about 15 or 16 per cent but it wants everyone else to accept a ceiling of 8 per cent-there may be 2 per cent for productivity and 2 per cent for cost-of-living increases. Controls, according to the Prime Minister, may last for three years and one thing which should be of concern to all of us is the indication by the Prime Minister-and now I am paraphrasing-that there is likely to be not less authority exercised in our times, but more. All these things have created an intolerable at mos-phere leading to less productivity and less profit.
It is the government's business to create a positive atmosphere in order to allow the private sector the opportunity to provide jobs, thus developing the economy. The budget could have been utilized to create this atmosphere, but the minister did not take advantage of his opportunity. He abdicated his responsibility in this regard. The government, in my humble submission, must get off the pot. It must say whether or not there is a meaningful role to be played by the private sector.
For the past five years we have been living in a vacuum-benign neglect. We must get together with business, labour, consumer groups and other levels of government to determine a game plan. We have to determine what ought to be our real growth; what our aims ought to be. How we can reduce our export deficits which today stand at some $5 billion? How can we place greater emphasis on the need for higher productivity? We must determine some kind of industrial strategy in co-operation with all these sectors of the economy, and outline the roles each have to play. These are important questions, Mr. Speaker, but the budget was totally silent with regard to them.
In terms of bringing about a climate of confidence the budget was an unqualified disaster, given the very serious economic problems we face. The budget will be known for what it failed to do rather than for what it accomplished. It showed, as I said earlier, that the government is bankrupt in terms of policy, is devoid of any constructive ideas. The economy, which needed a shot in the arm, instead got a shot in the head.
I see my time is about to expire, Mr. Speaker. If hon. members would agree to allow me about three more minutes I would have time to finish my remarks. I would appreciate that consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I am sure hon. members will agree to the hon. member's request. Is there consent to allow the hon. member to complete his remarks?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall not take the time of the House unduly but I think we should be apprized of the fact that, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) has indicated, there could have been a cut of one billion dollars had proper restraints been exercised. I will not spell out the details, but what was significant was that he was prepared to give a tax credit of $250 million, of which $100 million would go to those earning $8,000 or less, the remainder to be given on the basis of a scale to those
The Budget-Mr. Alexander
earning between $8,000 and $16,000, most of which would go directly into consumer spending, adding nearly three tenths of one per cent to the gross that would occur with such a tax credit. There would be a considerable impact on domestically generated demand, and thus on jobs.
A further proposal made by the hon. member for York-Simcoe involved a $100 million tax incentive program adjusted to ensure the greatest benefits to regions where disparity is greatest. That is what is bothering my friends from the Atlantic provinces. There has been no recognition of the need in areas where disparities are greatest. Not only would this incentive encourage the construction of research facilities, particularly in areas of regional disparity, but job opportunities for skilled workers would increase as well, as would those for the unskilled workers required to support the plant.
My hon. friend from York-Simcoe also advocated export incentives and promotions to the tune of some $75 million. This was part of the savings we were going to get by way of restraint. Then we would shift the priorities. In fact we had about $450 million left over in order to reduce other deficits. Other proposals included a program of tax incentives to encourage exports, and government spending directed to gain export markets, primarily for the benefit of small businessmen.
The government has time in which to reflect upon what it is doing right now. I refer particularly to the proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in terms of their impact upon job creation. I am not all that happy when I hear the minister say "We are going to extend LIP." That's good but it is only short term. All those jobs will sooner or later be eliminated. What we need is an approach along the lines the Economic Council of Canada indicated with respect to the $1 billion savings. I hope the ministers are looking at this suggestion with interest because we just cannot continue these ad hoc approaches, these piecemeal attacks on unemployment insurance. People want to work, but somebody has to create an atmosphere favourable to job creation. In this regard some attention will have to be paid to the question of whether in fact the government is interested in the private sector.
The musings of the Prime Minister have made a lot of people extremely nervous. Is there one rule for the public sector and another for the private sector? This is what we shall be looking at. Before the minister brings in his bill for first reading, what is to happen in the interim? Is there to be a serious effort to get away from this ad hoc approach to the serious problems I have outlined? As I said, this country should not have 760,000 people out of work.
The government has stolen our policy. We are not going to quibble about that; it is to be expected from that gang. Our policy was that the Unemployment Insurance Act, in terms of the minimum qualifying period, should allow entrance after 12 insured weeks, and since we have advocated such a policy since June, 1971, or prior thereto we have no alternative but to vote against the NDP motion which, in effect, does not want any meaningful amendment to be made to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The NDP want people to rely on unemployment just as the government does, and this is the matter we object to most strenuously.


The Budget-Mr. Cafik

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this is the first budget brought forward by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald)-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the last.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will have to wait and see about that-I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his budget. He faced, as I think everyone in the country appreciates, an enormous dilemma in preparing a budget at a time of high inflation and high unemployment, a budget that would be satisfactory to all Canadians. He has met this challenge quite well from my standpoint. He has brought forward measures that I believe will stimulate the economy without over-heating it; it will be sufficient to improve employment opportunities in a significant way without at the same time undermining the anti-inflation program.
The key elements of the budget that I would briefly touch on before dealing with the primary issue that I want to deal with in my speech today are as follows. First of all the amendments to the anti-inflation program dealing with the price side are very important steps in the right direction so as to create a better degree of credibility for the whole anti-inflation program, which I think has been launched with some degree of success to date. But by and large the public have felt, rightly or wrongly, that the greatest emphasis has been on the wages side. Quite frankly I think there has been equal emphasis and even more stringent control on the price side, though it may not have been very visible.
The rulings of the Anti-Inflation Board have been primarily on the wages side, and this has created the impression that the controls on prices are in fact not working. This is not the case. The change proposed in the budget will create, I think, a better climate where the public at large will come to realize that we are very serious about fighting inflation, and particularly about controlling prices in Canada.
The other steps announced in the budget to inhibit increased government expenditure are, of course, welcome. For instance there is the proposal in the budget that in the year 1976-77 and in 1977-78 the actual increase in government expenditures will be kept below the increase in the Gross National Product projections. This is something many people have wanted to see happen for some time. We will now be moving in this direction, and in terms of getting a handle on the economic situation in this country these are extremely important steps. However, I would enter one caveat, one word of caution, and that is that we should be very careful that we ourselves as parliamentarians do not over-react and paint out ourselves into a corner of restraint in terms of government expenditures, because this will render it impossible for us to provide good government.
There is no doubt that governments have to spend money for socially desirable purposes, such as transfer payments and the basic necessities required by our citizens. I think it would be very unwise not to bear in mind our responsibilities in this regard. We should not overreact to people who have a distorted view of the impact of

government expenditures on the economy. These people seem to think that if a government spends a dollar, it is a different dollar from the dollar spent by the private sector, it is true that private sector expenditures, like all expenditures, stimulate the economy, but the fact of the matter is that a dollar is a dollar. When money is needed in the economy it really matters not where it comes. The fact is that it is needed, and it has to be provided in one way or another. When the sector is not able to provide adequate job opportunities or stimulation of the economy, then the government itself has to intervene. However, it should do so only when there is a demonstrable reason for so doing.
I am also very pleased with the steps announced in the budget to improve the measure of assistance given the private sector, particularly the small business community. Perhaps we should move even further in this connection. I have spoken many times in this House about some of the programs in Industry, Trade and Commerce, where we should shift the emphasis from grants, interest free loans or forgiveable loans into straight loans to the private sector, particularly to small businessmen, so as to provide them with the growth capital they require to meet the needs of themselves and the rest of the community. More money could be loosened up in this way without increasing government expenditure one iota.
The basic change proposed in the budget to increase the rate of taxation for small business people from $100,000 to $150,000, and the cumulative figure from $550,000 to $750,000, is going to provide a considerable incentive and stimulation to the small industrial sector and business community. When we think of the private sector many of us think almost exclusively in terms of multinational corporations and the giants of the business community. The simple fact of the matter is that the small businessman who employs a small number of people really provides more jobs and stimulation of the economy than all the multinationals put together. This is why providing assistance to these entrepreneurs and business people who have the incentive to move forward is very important.
I think the tariff changes that benefit consumers are very worth while. I have some reservations about the tariff cuts that relate to farm products because of my deep concern for the well-being of farmers. We must continue to have an adequate farming base in this country, and I do not think it is useful to achieve low prices for foodstuffs if this dries up the very source of these commodities because the farmers do not have an adequate incentive to produce food.
I think the energy conservation proposals were a bit of a surprise but quite useful in terms of increasing taxes progressively on heavy cars, thus bringing about some fuel economies. The measures to provide a two year tax writeoff for equipment used in the private sector and by municipalities to convert industrial municipal waste into productive energy sources are also worth while.
One matter that concerns me about energy and energy sources is the price of oil and petroleum products. I have mentioned on a number of occasions the reservations that I have about increases in the price of fuel and oil products, which to a very significant extent are designed to assist the exploration activities of the multinational corporations. I realize there are many safeguards to ensure that


this money is spent in that area, and I am pleased that there are these safeguards. But I would rather see the additional money received by the multinationals transferred to the government itself, and that we establish an appropriate federal agency that would reinvest this money in exploration activity. In this way Canadians will personally have some kind of equity interest in the development that must take place.
It seems to me to be inappropriate to allow these advantages to the private sector when we, through tax measures and other means, are providing them access to the funds to be able to do that. I think we need a national development fund for this purpose, and I believe it would provide some degree of credibility to the increases in petroleum prices the public is so aggrieved about at the present time.
In addition I am delighted with the personal income tax changes, particularly the additional deductible allowance for child care. This is very important at a time of high inflation when often of necessity both parents have to work. The additional allowance for deductions for child care from $500 to $1,000 per year is a very important measure, with the maximum deduction being changed from $2,000 to $4,000 per year per family. This will provide considerable assistance to people in this income category and in this condition of need.
The deferred income changes in relation to registered and non-registered retirement savings plans are also worth while in that they really escalate these levels so those planning for retirement can plan for a retirement income more consistent with what retirement needs will be in the future because of inflation that has taken place in the past and is taking place at the present time. The proposal is to change the level for registered plans from $2,500 to $3,500 per year, which is a step in the right direction, and for non-registered plans from $4,000 to $5,500.
Let me now address myself to what I think is one of the most significant aspects of the budgetary proposals. I should like for a few minutes to talk about those proposals relating to the unemployment insurance plan and to job creation generally.
I for one am very pleased to see the remarriage of the manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission sections of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The divorce that took place during the Pearson days in respect of those two elements of the same department I thought at that time was unwise, and I have felt so ever since. I have been a strong advocate of the need for bringing these two elements back together so we can provide a one-stop service centre for those in need of this service. This will provide greater efficiency, and I hope that in some small way this will contribute to a reduction in federal government expenditures, as I am sure it will when this program is fully put into place. In addition to this there are other things that need to be done. One thing that concerns me greatly in connection with the unemployment insurance program today is its credibility, or to put it more accurately, in some quarters its lack of credibility.
The UIC program brought forward by the new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Mackasey), the Postmaster General, was a very important departure. It
The Budget-Mr. Cafik
was a program I supported very strongly at the time, not only in the House but at all stages. That does not mean anyone at that time felt it was a perfect answer to a difficult problem, because clearly perfect answers to problems of this magnitude are rarely arrived at, in the House of Commons or anywhere else in society. Nonetheless I supported it then.
I am a great admirer of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for the concern he has had for the lower income people in our society. I do not want to detract from that feeling by any remarks I am about to make now, and I am sure I will not do so.
Credibility in the program is extremely important. If the public views this program as a rip-off, which I really do not think it is, and if it views the program as providing a disincentive to work, then we as politicians have to deal with that perception. It is not good enough to deal with it only by citing statistics. I happen to think that this perception, that it does provide some disincentive to work, has some degree of justification, and we have to meet that. At the moment, on the basis of the information and statistics I have seen, much of which have been developed in recent days by the Department of Manpower and Immigration relating to the whole question of the eligibility period, I think are convincing.
The present rules in relation to eligibility, which require somebody to be attached to the work force for eight weeks, as far as I can make out, with the exception I believe of Holland, represent the lowest entrance requirement in any country in the world. That is my understanding, but that does not mean to say it is wrong for that reason. In countries like England, which is considered by many to be an excessively welfare state, the entrance requirement is 26 weeks, and all over Europe the entrance requirement ranges up to a year and sometimes more, but rarely less than the figure of 26 weeks. I have just quoted for England. We have a program before us today under which the entrance requirement is eight weeks. That is technically less than two months. It is a small attachment to the work force, there is no question about that. The proposal is to change that attachment, not to the figure in England or even the much higher figures in Europe, but in a very modest way from eight weeks to 12 weeks. There is a significant impact, but a modest one nonetheless.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) has cited some facts in this case and I am not going to review them all today. I am impressed by a number of them. First of all, I am told that 64 per cent of those with an attachment of between eight weeks and 11 weeks drop out of the labour force after drawing their benefits. If that is the fact, and at the moment I have no reason to question the validity of it, that is a very staggering fact. Let us compare that dropout rate with the average of those who collect unemployment insurance. We find that the over-all average is 13.5 per cent, and for those who have been covered by insurance for a 52-week period the average is 1.8 per cent. I think that is quite significant.
The cost ratio of benefit payments to those in this category of eight weeks to 11 weeks is 20 times the average cost ratio. This does not mean we have to change the program by virtue of that statistic, but it does indicate in terms of insurance principle that there is reason to believe we ought


The Budget-Mr. Cafik
to reconsider our approach in respect of such a short attachment to the work force.
I am informed that the savings involved here run into the hundreds of millions of dollars, and we ought to redirect these funds toward job creation. If that could be done effectively, particularly on a regional basis for the Atlantic provinces and other areas of high unemployment, we would be doing the wise thing. I have not met many unemployed people who would rather be unemployed than working. Our responsibility is to provide them with that kind of job opportunity. I am not convinced that the redirection of a modest $200 million or $300 million would in fact achieve that objective, but I think it would be a step in the right direction, although more has to be done.
It is really incredible in a society like ours, with all its wealth, its intelligence, its resources and so on, that we cannot find ways and means of more properly matching our labour force and job opportunities. We have to do that as best we can. I believe, therefore, that the changes being proposed in the UIC plan are worth-while changes. I think we have to do this in order to create credibility for the program so that the original UIC program will not die because people relate badly to it. I think that by the changes we would reduce the misuse of the law for personal gain.
Some people have argued that all we need do is tighten up on the administration and that would cover all the abuses which exist. I do not believe that. I believe we have to tighten up the administration in certain areas. However, the abuses which take place now are abuses within the law. These cannot truly be called abuses because people take advantage of the law which parliament gave them to use. If the law is wrong, if it provides a disincentive in some way which reduces the desire of people to get out and find work when they need income, then I think the law needs to be changed. I think the changes will provide more stability in employment patterns by forcing people to have longer attachment to the work force.
It is true it is not always possible for people to be attached to the work force for the period they would like. Obviously that is not possible in many areas. However, there is no doubt there are people drawing unemployment insurance after having been attached for eight weeks now because they do not want to work for more than the period required in order to become eligible for those benefits. I have known of such cases. I believe that although this may not be a widespread abuse it is something which ought to be corrected within the law.
I also believe more funds should be provided and targeted toward job creation. That is important. We also need to provide more funds and initiative in the area of upgrading job skills through mobility and retraining programs. The minister has indicated his intention in this regard. I support that move considerably. I think one further point in connection with the need for the creation of job opportunities is that we should have what I have advocated for a long time. This is what I would call a national advisory council, on education in relation to skills needed by our society in the future.

It seems to me, now that the Department of Manpower and Immigration is married to the UIC in one unit, we might well consider the advisability of sitting down and trying to determine in a sensible and reasonable way what job opportunities are anticipated in the future in all the various trades and professions, and non-trades and professions, not that anyone should have a mandatory requirement to be educated, to be streamed only into a particular area of need, but so that we might find a guidepost in respect of those who go to our universities and trade institutions so that a job would be available to them when they graduate a few years hence. This is done in other countries and I think it might be done to some extent here so that we do not end up training more people in one profession than society will require. I think this should be considered by the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
Furthermore, I believe a change in the formula for federal contributions into the UIC fund from the moving average which exists now on a national basis to an average on a regional basis would assist the department in directing funds and benefits into those target areas which require the benefits most, those areas of high unemployment. That would be a worth-while step which in some way would minimize the fear and concern many members of this House have in connection with the high levels of unemployment in their own regions and the impact of this particular program on that problem.
I also believe that the Department of Manpower should look very closely, with national bodies such as labour unions and so on, at appropriate methods of providing adequate apprenticeship programs within our society. I have a tendency to believe that far too many trades and even professions look upon apprenticeship programs, or even educational programs in such a way that they want to keep a closed shop to some extent to provide the maximum benefits to their own members. It seems to me that in the national interest we must ensure that such self-regulating bodies do not act in such a way as to deny job opportunities in skills and professions to many people in our population who at the present moment do not have an opportunity to enter into them. I think this is an important area of activity and one most appropriate for the consideration of the Department of Manpower.
I shall not continue any further in connection with the unemployment insurance program except to say that, on the basis of information I have, I believe it is important that we make adjustments in this program, not to destroy it but to preserve it, and to make sure that it does serve not only those people who are unemployed but all Canadians.
It would seem to me that by using our resources properly, which are contributed to in that plan by management, the employees, and the government, and that by earmarking those benefits in the right way we will serve all people in our society. I sincerely hope these proposals will play their role in providing more job opportunities and providing the kind of incentive we require in our labour force so that we may continue to have the kind of society we have had in the past number of years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the two topics I intend to discuss, I would like


to congratulate the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) for having been invited by the Prime Minister to assume the responsibilities of Minister of Finance. From the economic and financial standpoint, it is one of the most important departments in the Canadian administration. The Minister of Finance has very heavy responsibilities, and a lot of courage was necessary to agree to make a speech which shows a lot of timidity in attacking the real causes of inflation, a generator of unemployment with all the attendant problems.
Mr. Speaker, if we look back at past budget speeches, we see that government policy has been changing from year to year. First the government fought inflation while taking the chance of seeing unemployment rise; the next year, the government conceived a policy to fight unemployment, while risking a surge in the inflation rates. This year, the new Minister of Finance is offering us a new formula when he says:
We believe that the problems of unemployment and inflation must be solved together.
I am in complete agreement with this attitude. However, no new formula has been announced which would let us hope that an answer will be found to these two problems caused by an outmoded and distorted financial system which no longer corresponds to the economic realities of this day and age. To be fair to the minister, I must admit that the increase in the profit ceilings for small businesses will be an incentive for those who make considerable efforts to maintain their business in operation in spite of all the difficulties caused by legislation which is becoming more and more obscure and regulations which complement this legislation and are prepared by qualified public servants, but do not always reflect the true feelings of the legislators. I am convinced that if we took the trouble of really attacking the main causes of the problem, we could improve the economic situation of our country, and consequently that of all Canadian citizens.
As concerns the fiscal benefits granted to small businesses, I think that they are well deserved, and that they will promote further development. I always support private enterprise, and when I see that the government develops formulas and benefits to help the development of private enterprise, I am convinced that we are on the right track because the private sector allows businessmen to use their energy, develop their talent and prepare a way to encourage others who would be tempted to do more.
An aspect which the Minister of Finance did not really mention is that of benefits for single dwelling owners. We have been asking for a number of years that property taxes be deductible from the income tax. I believe that if this formula were approved, it would be a step in the right direction and would promote residential construction, create employment and assist home ownership.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to talk about a very important subject on which the minister did not dwell sufficiently in his budget. I mean the farming industry, and more particularly the dairy industry and the cattle industry. Dairy producers are now going through a very difficult crisis which threatens to eliminate a number of producers who have answered in good faith to the appeal of government authorities.
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in recent years governments at all levels have advocated a policy for larger farms assuming that they would be more viable. The government has even gone further in encouraging farmers to move along that line by increasing loans granted to those who wanted to buy a farm, build up a herd and mechanize their operations.
Building upon that policy for larger farms, a great many farmers got into debt for years and now the federal government refuses to recognize it is responsible for the higher dairy production and to fully assume its responsibilities. An increase in dairy production was to be expected with the launching of this policy for quasi-commercial type of arms. In 1973-74 and 1974-75, the government urged dairy producers to boost their production. A number of producers answered to that requirement by raising a good many heifers that have or will become milking cows.
The government told dairy producers that they are themselves responsible for this situation. However, what the government does not say and should say is that in 1975 Canada imported $56 million worth of dairy products and exported for $36 million-hence a deficit of $20 million.
In the whole, when it comes to farm products such as cattle on the hoof or carcasses, dairy products, eggs, veal, lamb, pork, horse and chicken meat, from a favourable commercial balance of $1 million in 1973, Canada accumulated a commercial deficit of $52 million in 1975. In fact, here is where we stand how: in April 1975, the levy for export costs was 45 cents a hundredweight. The support price was $11.02, the actual price was $10.52.
In April 1976, the export levy went to $1.35 a hundredweight and the support price was raised to $11.45 which reduced the actual price at the producer level at $10.10-a reduction of 47 cents a hundredweight. Furthermore, the quota subjected to subsidies was established at $9.5 billion. In Quebec it will result in a 16 per cent reduction from last year deliveries. The surplus will be penalized to the tune of $8.60 a hundredweight on the farm. But if the producer still delivers more milk in April 1976 than he did twelve months earlier, less 16 per cent, there will be a penalty of $8.60, plus transportation costs, plus the cost of publicity and the joint program which will cost in fact $9.13 a hundredweight.
A producer who marketed 20,000 pounds of milk in April 1975 will see his quota reduced by 16 per cent, or 3,200 pounds. Then his deliveries for 1976 will be restricted to 16,800 pounds. If he is paid $8.50 a hundredweight by the plant plus a $2.66 subsidy and less exportation and other costs, he will get $1,564 for the rest, the 3,200 pounds on which there will be a penalty of $9.13 a hundredweight and he will have to pay a penalty of $292.
If in April 1976, the same producer has turned out, as most of them do, 4,000 additional pounds of milk as compared with 1975 and if he delivers this milk to the plant, he will have to pay on this additional amount a penalty of $9.13 a hundredweight, that is $365.20. The aggregate of penalties will amount to $657.20, and therefore he will in fact be left with only $906.80 for a total production of 24,000


The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert
pounds of milk, that is $3.78 a hundredweight. To this the producer will have to add his production cost for the amount of milk produced on which he must pay a penalty of $4.13 a hundredweight.
This amounts in fact to a direct tax on the producer's gross income, the most appalling I have ever seen. This is only one example, Mr. Speaker, Some producers will lose a few thousand dollars this year. Their financial status will be bad, worse than last year, as a result of this reduction in income. And all this is reward for the work that the farmer, as the owner, his wife and children have strived to do.
This is their reward. How can the problem be solved? We must not simply note the facts, we must suggest solutions. Therefore, as a responsible member and spokesman for a large number of people affected by this measure-because my constituents are primarily farmers-I say that the answer of the government was that producers are responsible for this situation and they can manage to solve their own problems.
First of all, have we made all necessary efforts to promote the consumption of dairy products in Canada? Are substitutes not cornering an overly large part of the market? Could anything be done in this regard? Second, why not reinstate the subsidy on the quart of fresh milk? This measure was good in 1973, it would still be good today. It would contribute to increase the consumption of fresh milk and to cut down the substantial surplus of fresh milk and that of industrial milk as well.
In 16 months, in 1973 and 1974, the government paid $108 million in subsidies throughout Canada. That is much more than the industrial milk producers are now asking as compensation for loss of income, for submitting to the quotas the government has decided will apply this year. I shall now speak of the distribution of milk in schools. To achieve that, a practical way of doing so should be found: the government should ask its researchers and economists to work on the project. CIDA could also absorb some of the costs with part of the billion dollar budget it is allotted to help developing countries.
I really believe it is unreasonable to pour down the drain a product Providence enables us to have in Canada. Let us take care for, if we waste too much, some day may come when we are short of the basic necessities and we, in turn, become a famished people. It is unreasonable to ask that category of workers to accept lower incomes in 1976 when the government recognizes the necessity of increases for all other groups in our society to enable them to face the cost of living. Farm producers live in the same country as the others, and also bear the burden of the soaring cost of living. Canada, as compared with many other countries, devotes a smaller portion of its budget to agriculture. Producers are willing to agree with lowering their production.
But this requires that the government give them compensation for the loss of revenue relative to last year. This the Canadian government did in 1969, when we helped the prairie grain farmers faced with an overproduction of grain. The federal government spent $100 million to compensate for the revenue lost by western farmers in not seeding a certain acreage. This week, the government hit eastern farmers on the head, especially those in the prov-

ince of Quebec, with the partial cancellation of the subsidy on feed grain transportation. I have here a telegram received yesterday from the milling association of the province of Quebec, begging the government to reconsider, because of the tremendous impact on the cattle industry.
In their name I ask the Minister of Finance to consider that request and take corrective measures before it is too late. Since Quebec accounts for almost 50 per cent of the total Canadian milk production and since this is the main farm industry in Quebec, that province will be more severely hit. The last two agricultural initiatives by the federal government are giving fuel to the arguments in favour of separation. Sensible people who firmly believe in federalism are seriously shaken by such measures. This is not an off the cuff suggestion. I have received communications to support that indication.
Last night on television, the Quebec Minister of Agriculture was quite categorical on the subject. Those who heard him must share my view. I will not quote him, but the import of his statement was that he could be anything but satisfied and he did not accept the government's decisions.
So, Mr. Speaker, I beg the government to be more flexible and to accept to spend a few million dollars to save the dairy industry from this disaster. Measures must be taken immediately to hearten the producers who send their milk cows to the slaughter house, which will inevitably lead us to shortages.
Mr. Speaker, during the few minutes I have left before the vote, I would like to deal with the second subject, which came to my mind after I read a release which the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) sent to hon. members on April 28, 1975, and which reads:
... The Minister of State for Urban Affairs, the Hon. Barney Danson, and the Minister of Municipal Affairs and of the Environment, who applies the rules of the Quebec Housing Corporation, Dr. Victor C. Goldbloom, have announced that 38 construction projects for 1,435 housing units ...
. .. will be built. Then the release says:
Loans amounting to $30,193,489, refundable on a 50-year period at 103/s per cent, have been granted by the CMHC pursuant to the agreement of 1974 ... These loans cover nearly 90 per cent of the construction costs of the projects and the balance will be provided by the Quebec Housing Corporation.
As two communities situated in my riding participate in this program, I asked a question to the minister, which is recorded in the order paper, and we were given the answer on February 23, 1976.
The question was: Were loans made in the riding of Bellechasse, in the municipalities of Saint-Damien and Saint-VAUier, to the Quebec Housing Corporation for building 30 housing units in Saint-Damien and 20 in Saint-Vallier? In answer I was told that indeed an amount of $537,863 was provided for 30 units in Saint-Damien and $292,473 for 20 units in Saint-Vallier. The interest rate, as I just said is 103/s per cent. The loans will be repaid over an amortization period of 50 years.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I did some figuring and on the basis of the figures I came up with if the Quebec Housing Corporation repays $57,617.24 a year over 50 years, it will pay $2,342,999 to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation-the price of 120 units. And older people will get only 30 of them, the 90 others going to finance. So, on the


basis of those figures, and I had them checked, I am told they are right. The Quebec Housing Corporation will have to pay back the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will have to pay back the government which will have to pay back those who control-the credit makers-and mint the credit of this nation.
So high finance is well organized, it uses government to put people in debt, to impose obligations upon them, and they do not have to put out money. So I say it is a method of financing that is too costly. We cannot afford to pay that financing-for $537,863 Canadian taxpayers will have to shell out $2,880,862. I feel this is usury. I made the calculations with the same figures provided by the minister at a simple interest of 103/s per cent, not compound interest- and that is compound interest. Considering the cost of compound interest in the public sector, I am beginning to understand why Canada's debt since 1867 went from $75 million to $55 billion today. That is why we have a financing system in the public sector that burdens federal government budgets, and it is the same thing with the provinces and the municipalities.
At simple interest, even 103/a per cent, the repayment would be only $1,423,667.39 that is $1,961,530.39 in all with capital. That is according to the debt credit system under which we are run. With the credit system based on what we believe to be true, that credit belongs to society with true social credit and of which only the administration costs would have to be paid, we would pay back $10,757.26 a year on the capital and we would pay administration costs at 1 Vi per cent. It means that at the end of the year through credit created by the Bank of Canada instead of chartered banks, because one must recognize that the public sector is different from the private sector, the money market would be freed for the private sector, interest rates would go down. Inflation would be fought effectively and so would unemployment. And I think it would be a good thing to accept that formula; that is what I am asking the Minister of Finance.

Thursday, June 3, 1976
